Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Nobody shares how behind they are. Say plainly that this is a tool, not a cure for a hard semester. A student frozen for weeks should hear that a counselor can help.

Every student in the room

Some students carry a lot at home (siblings, jobs, two homes, a parent who is struggling), so name that "too much" can come from life outside school, and keep every example invented.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students learn why a long to-do list leads to freezing, and practice the way out: pick one thing, make it smaller, and tie it to a moment that already happens. Nobody shares how behind they are.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 3 minOne word for your to-do list
  2. 5 minThe freeze
  3. 5 minSmall, specific plans work, and make it smaller
  4. 5 minShrink it: turn and talk, share out
  5. 12 minFirst tiny steps: Zoe, Ben, Ines, Theo
  6. 5 minHook it to something that already happens
  7. 5 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

One word, the freeze, make it smaller, two of the four scenes, hook it to a moment, and the close.

Before you teach
Shrink the task, not the student.

The message is that the task is too big, not that the student is lazy or disorganized. Avoid "just get it done" or "you have plenty of time." Say: "Make it so small it feels silly. Then start."

Keep the cards invented.

Use the four cards, not students' own situations. Nobody says how many assignments they're missing out loud.

Wanting to go home is real.

The Theo card is about wanting to leave a trip early. Some students have strong separation worries. Keep it gentle: wanting home makes sense, and small steps of staying a little longer help. A student who often leaves school or trips early is worth a quiet word with a counselor.

Underwater is different from busy.

A student who has stopped turning in work, isn't sleeping, or seems hopeless needs more than a tip. Check in privately after advisory and tell a counselor that day. Disclosures go to a counselor. No screening questions in the group.

ADHD and learning plans.

Some students have ADHD or a learning plan. One small step is a good fit for them, and it doesn't replace their supports. Point them to learning support if a list never seems to shrink.

Model it.

Share your own version: the email you avoided for a week, and the tiny first step that finally got it sent. It gives students permission to admit they freeze too.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

"Too much" isn't only school.

Students may care for siblings, work after school, translate for family, or split time between homes. Name life outside school as part of the load, without asking anyone to share theirs.

Homes look different.

"Clean your room" assumes a room of your own. Keep examples flexible: a desk, a shelf, a corner, a bag.

Families handle help differently.

In some families asking a teacher for more time feels disrespectful, or asking a parent for help isn't possible. Offer several adults: advisor, teacher, coach, counselor, learning support.

Neurodivergent students.

Students with ADHD or autism may freeze more often or need the steps written down. Concrete, visible steps help everyone. Avoid treating disorganization as a character flaw.

Wanting to be home.

Some students and families value closeness to home, and some students have real reasons to worry about home while they're away. Treat wanting home as normal, not babyish.

Language.

English learners can write their one step in any language, or draw it.

What the research says

Across 94 studies, people who made if-then plans ("When X happens, I'll do Y") reached their goals much more often than people who only set the goal. The effect was medium to large.

Gollwitzer & Sheeran, Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, 2006

A 2025 update of the same research, covering 642 tests, found if-then plans help across many kinds of goals and people.

Sheeran, Listrom & Gollwitzer, European Review of Social Psychology, 2025

Behavioral activation, scheduling small doable activities, works about as well as cognitive therapy for low mood. Action tends to come before motivation, not after.

Ekers et al., PLoS ONE, 2014; Richards et al., The Lancet, 2016

For adults with ADHD, skills training that breaks tasks into small steps and puts them on a calendar improved time management and organization more than a support group did.

Solanto et al., American Journal of Psychiatry, 2010

Procrastination is mostly a way of avoiding bad feelings about a task, not a time-management problem.

Sirois & Pychyl, Social and Personality Psychology Compass, 2013

For children and teens with separation anxiety, gradual practice staying a little longer is the core of effective treatment; avoidance tends to make the worry stronger.

Walkup et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2008
